# Ten snapshots were generated by several CLI invocations at once

**Date:** 2026-08-28
**Status:** an instrument measurement, not a round. No rule changed, no round is
accepted or rejected by it. Closes [#120].

## What was wrong

`run.py` is strictly sequential: one `subprocess.run`, then one
`save_snapshot`, per cell. A reader of a snapshot would reasonably conclude that
at most one CLI call was ever in flight. For ten committed snapshots that is
false. Rounds 16 and 17 record it in prose — `metadata.sharded` says "one case
per process at 5-way concurrency, merged" — and the other eight say nothing at
all, because each shard process wrote its own file and the merge happened
afterwards by hand.

Reconstructing each call's window as `[generated_at - duration_ms,
generated_at]` and sweeping for maximum overlap, grouped by arm and generation
day so a carried arm is not mixed with a fresh one:

| snapshot | arm | day | n | wall | summed | ratio | max in flight |
|---|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `round-17` | laconic | 08-12 | 340 | 24.0 m | 107.5 m | 4.49 | **5** |
| `round-20` | laconic | 08-14 | 440 | 26.5 m | 115.4 m | 4.36 | **6** |
| `round-18` | laconic | 08-13 | 440 | 35.4 m | 152.9 m | 4.32 | **5** |
| `round-17` | laconic | 08-13 | 100 | 10.3 m | 42.6 m | 4.13 | **5** |
| `baseline-arm-n10` | baseline | 08-14 | 190 | 16.9 m | 65.3 m | 3.87 | **6** |
| `round-18-arbitration` | laconic | 08-13 | 40 | 7.2 m | 10.9 m | 1.51 | **2** |
| `design-discrimination` | baseline | 08-12 | 80 | 27.8 m | 40.8 m | 1.47 | **4** |
| `design-discrimination` | word-compression | 08-12 | 80 | 28.4 m | 40.1 m | 1.41 | **4** |
| `baseline-arm-n10` | baseline | 08-12 | 60 | 25.2 m | 30.8 m | 1.22 | **3** |
| `round-01-n10-v4` | baseline | 08-12 | 30 | 13.2 m | 15.2 m | 1.15 | **3** |
| `round-01-n10-v4` | word-compression | 08-12 | 30 | 13.8 m | 14.9 m | 1.08 | **3** |
| `round-01-n10-v4` | terse-control | 08-12 | 30 | 13.5 m | 14.7 m | 1.09 | **3** |
| `round-01-n10-v4` | laconic | 08-12 | 60 | 26.9 m | 29.0 m | 1.08 | **3** |
| `round-16` | laconic | 08-12 | 440 | 277.1 m | 149.3 m | 0.54 | **5** |
| `round-19` | laconic | 08-13 | 440 | 210.1 m | 152.3 m | 0.72 | **5** |
| `quality-rates-design` | laconic | 08-12 | 180 | 667.5 m | 90.5 m | 0.14 | **3** |

A ratio above 1 is the same fact without a sweep: more CLI-seconds were consumed
than elapsed. Rounds 16 and 19 have ratios below 1 only because their arms
contain long idle gaps, and their peak overlap of 5 still shows the concurrency.
The `round-01-n10-v4` rows are the 2026-08-12 control batch that
`--carry-arms-from` copies into every round from 16 to 24; the sweep charges it
to the snapshot that generated it rather than to each of the nine that carry it.

The reconstruction is a floor in two ways. `duration_ms` is the CLI's figure for
the attempt that was recorded, so a cell that failed and was retried contributes
one window where two calls happened. And `generated_at` has one-second
resolution, so a call ending in the same second the next begins reads as
sequential.

**Everything else is sequential.** Rounds 14 and 15 and both round-15 holdout
files, and every round from 21 to 29, sweep to a maximum of 1.

## Does the execution regime move a measurement?

The archive contains no pair of batches matched on rules, cases, models and CLI
that differs only in regime, so no clean estimate exists. What it does contain is
one contrast where the rules text is byte-identical: `rules_cksum` 3980812364 was
generated sequentially on 08-11 (rounds 14, 15, 15-replication) and again at
6-way concurrency on 08-14 (round 20). Rounds 14 and 15 against each other are
the matching sequential-to-sequential control — the same comparison with the
regime held fixed.

**On `output_tokens`, the metric every token gate reads, the regime change does
nothing the batch change does not already do.** Per-cell medians, matched on case
and model:

| contrast | cells | median shift | median abs shift | cells up | sign test |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| round 14 to round 15, both sequential | 34 | +0.8% | 5.5% | 20 of 34 | p = 0.392 |
| round 15 to round 20, sequential to 6-way | 38 | −0.1% | 5.4% | 18 of 38 | p = 0.871 |
| round 14 to round 20, sequential to 6-way | 34 | +0.2% | 4.3% | 18 of 34 | p = 0.864 |

Two batches of identical rules differ by about 5% per cell in either direction
whether or not the regime changed with them.

**Per-call latency did not inflate either**, which is the direct test of the
contention mechanism: median `duration_ms` moves −6.3% from round 15 to round 20
and +3.8% from round 14 to round 15. Median `num_turns` is unchanged in both.

**The one-turn rate does differ between batches, and it moves in opposite
directions on the two sides of the contrast.** Sonnet design cases, byte-identical
rules within each row:

| rules | sequential | concurrent | Fisher |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| licence, 3980812364 | 49/130 (37.7%) | 45/80 (56.2%) | p = 0.0102 |
| master, 1830906901 | 12/30 (40.0%) | 19/120 (15.8%) | p = 0.0058 |

Concurrency raises the rate on one side and lowers it on the other, both at
p < 0.011. One mechanism cannot do both. This is the between-round
overdispersion `one-turn-investigation.md` already measures at phi = 3.03 and
phi = 4.49, and the regime is a passenger on it, not its cause. Both contrasts
are also cross-date and cross-CLI, so neither is clean on its own; what the
opposite signs rule out is the simple story that running several invocations at
once inflates the one-turn rate.

## Re-reading the affected comparisons

**`design-discrimination.json`, the evidence admitting the three [#88] cases —
unaffected.** Both of its arms were generated inside the same 4-way batch, and
the two arms of a cell are a median 40 seconds apart, so the regime is
common-mode across the contrast the file exists to make. `run.py` loops arms
innermost precisely so that arms are sampled at adjacent moments; that property
is what protects an arm-versus-arm comparison from anything the batch is doing.

**`round-01-n10-v4.json`, the master baseline — unaffected in the same way, more
weakly.** Its arms sit in the same day and the same declared regime, but a
median 39 minutes apart rather than 40 seconds, because they were generated in
separate passes over one day.

**The n=10 baseline correction ([`baseline-arm-n10.md`](baseline-arm-n10.md)) —
the conclusion survives, and the regime is the wrong suspect.** That document
reports nine cells changing the sign of their laconic-versus-baseline delta and
attributes it to sampling error in a five-draw control. Splitting the baseline
arm at the rep boundary and asking whether the two halves came from the same
batch separates the two explanations:

| half-to-half contrast | cells | median abs shift | largest |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| both halves inside the 08-12 4-way batch | 6 | 19.7% | `design-upload`/haiku +125.5% |
| reps 0-4 versus the 08-14 6-way batch | 38 | 6.8% | `design-audit-log`/haiku +69.0% |

**The two largest movements in the whole correction happen inside a single
batch, at one regime.** `design-upload`/haiku (556 to 1254) and
`design-cache`/haiku (730 to 1457) are reps 0-4 against reps 5-9 of the same
4-way pass on 2026-08-12; nothing about the execution regime changed between
them. Five draws was simply thin, exactly as the document concluded. The cells
that do cross a regime boundary move less, not more.

**Round-to-round comparisons that cross the boundary — two, both already
rejected.** The laconic arm is sequential through round 15, concurrent for rounds
16 to 20, and sequential again from round 21, so exactly two consecutive-round
comparisons straddle it:

- **Round 15 to round 16**, `quality_fails` 31 to 28 against a registered
  threshold of 18. Rejected at p = 0.397. Concurrency can only have widened the
  noise on a number that did not come close to its threshold.
- **Round 20 to round 21.** Round 20 rejected on its own counters against round
  19, which is also concurrent, so the round's verdict does not cross the
  boundary. What does cross it is the one-turn contrast
  `one-turn-investigation.md` draws — round 20's licence at 45/80 against round
  21's master at 26/80 — and that comparison is already reported as
  non-significant once overdispersion is applied (binomial p = 0.0025, phi = 3.03
  p = 0.082, phi = 4.49 p = 0.154). It is now also known to be cross-regime, which
  is one more reason not to read it as a rules effect.

**Rounds 16 to 19 against each other — unaffected.** All four are concurrent at
5 or 6, so the regime is common-mode across every comparison among them.

## What the harness does now

1. **Every run records which invocation produced it.** `run.py` stamps a
   `generator` id — timestamp plus pid — onto each run, per-run rather than
   per-snapshot for the reason [#80] gives: a snapshot-level stamp is written once
   at creation and then inherited by every later pass, including one a different
   process made. Two ids inside one arm and day is two processes, stated instead
   of reconstructed.
2. **Every snapshot carries the reconstructed number.**
   `metadata.max_runs_in_flight`, recomputed on every write over the runs the
   snapshot generated, so it is right after a merge of shard files the writing
   process never saw.
3. **Concurrency is allowed, and has a flag.** It is roughly 4x faster and each
   process owns its own file, so nothing races on a write. `run.py --concurrency
   N` declares how many processes a round is being generated by and records it as
   `metadata.concurrency_declared`; a resume keeps the widest declaration the file
   has carried. What is no longer allowed is an *undeclared* regime: the pass
   prints a warning when its own timestamps reconstruct to more invocations than
   it declared.
4. **A checker, and a report line.** `python3 evals/bench/concurrency.py` sweeps
   every committed snapshot and exits non-zero on an arm-day exceeding its
   declaration; it produced the tables above. `report.py` prints
   `Generation regime` in the provenance header of every report, computed from the
   runs, so a snapshot written before any of this still discloses how it was
   produced.

`tests/test_bench.py` pins the ten-snapshot affected set, so a new name appearing
in it means a round was generated concurrently and this document needs
re-reading.
